comments.author: saed ‎
comments.comment:
One practical test I’d add: run the same agent task with a malicious tool result buried 3-5 steps deep, not just in the first prompt.

A lot of agent failures show up only after the model has built trust in the workflow. The security eval needs to test state drift, not just single-turn refusal behavior.

comments.author: Sukaimi Sukri
comments.comment: The underrated test is whether the system can admit “I know the rule, but I don’t know today’s hours” before it answers. A good harness should carry date, location, calendar exceptions, source freshness, and confidence separately, because mixing those into one prompt makes failures harder to debug. What do you log when the setup gets an answer right for the wrong reason?

comments.author: Raahul Seshadri
comments.comment: The prompt is part of the decision system, not just an input string. One pattern I like is forcing the model to write the decision memo twice: once optimizing for speed, once optimizing for trust, then extract the assumptions that actually changed. That usually tells you more than the recommendation itself.

comments.author: Antoine Tilloy
comments.comment: The hardest part may not be raw model capability, it may be verification latency. If AI can generate 100 candidate proofs or implementations fast, the scarce skill shifts to building tests, invariants, formal checks, and taste filters that fail bad work cheaply. I’d be curious where you think theoretical research hits that verification wall first.
